text: "Trapper Keeper" is the twelfth episode of the fourth season of the animated series South Park and the 60th episode overall, being the 13th in production order for Season 4. It originally aired on Comedy Central in the United States on November 15, 2000, and was completed at approximately nine in the morning on that day, only days after the 2000 United States presidential election concluded. The episode features a man from the future, named BSM-471 and referred to as "Bill Cosby," who seeks to destroy Cartman's advanced Trapper Keeper, a device that is destined to gain sentience and evolve into a supercomputer capable of conquering the world and erasing humanity. The Trapper Keeper's storyline is a parody of the Terminator films and the anime movie Akira, with its ability to absorb and transform into various electronic devices echoing the eponymous entity in the 1958 film The Blob. Meanwhile, Mr. Garrison, now teaching kindergarten, holds a class president election where Kyle's brother Ike, admitted two years early due to supposed intelligence despite not speaking properly, runs against Filmore, resulting in a tie that is broken by a vote from a little girl named Flora. Flora initially hesitates but ultimately chooses Ike, prompting Filmore's supporters to demand recounts and call in Rosie O'Donnell, who protests the results. Lawyers are brought in, extensive paperwork is filed, and protracted meetings occur, leading Filmore to concede the election, stating "this game is stupid." The class then proceeds to fingerpaint, delighting Mr. Garrison. Kyle shows his friends a Dawson's Creek Trapper Keeper, which Cartman boasts about having upgraded to a special "Ultra Keeper Futura S 2000" with features like a television, music player with voice recognition, OnStar, and self-hybridization. Kyle accuses Cartman of buying it to make him envious. A mysterious white man, "Bill Cosby," attempts to steal the Trapper Keeper, succeeds by purchasing Cartman's trust, and explains his mission: to prevent the binder from becoming a world-conquering supercomputer. He destroys the Trapper Keeper, but Cartman buys another and refuses to let it be destroyed. The Trapper Keeper then integrates into Cartman's computer and belongings, absorbing him into a giant, cybernetic blob-like monster resembling Akira, which kills Kenny, destroys Cartman's house, and heads to Cheyenne Mountain to absorb its computer system. Bill Cosby warns that if the Trapper Keeper merges with the military base's computer, it will become unstoppable. Kyle sneaks into the hybrid through a ventilation pipe, but is incapacitated before he can disable it. Rosie O'Donnell appears, yells at the Trapper Keeper for blocking the road, and is absorbed, causing the creature to become sick. Kyle is freed and disconnects the Trapper Keeper's CPU, causing it to lose power and release Cartman and a deceased O'Donnell as it collapses. Bill Cosby then disappears, and Stan tells Cartman to thank Kyle, who has saved his life. Cartman begins to speak to Kyle but is cut off before finishing. The episode parodies the 2000 United States presidential election, with state results on election night showing George W. Bush with 246 electoral votes and Al Gore with 255, while Florida's 25 electoral votes were too close to call and ultimately decided the outcome after a recount. New Mexico and Oregon were later called in Gore's favor. The controversy involved disputed Florida results, a recount process, and the unusual situation where the winner received fewer popular votes than the loser. The episode's election subplot was not originally included, only a scene involving Ike attending kindergarten, and was added to parody the election's absurdity. The main Trapper Keeper plot was written before the election, but the election storyline was added to reflect the controversy. Trey Parker and Matt Stone, the co-creators, said the election controversy was "kids' stuff" and that the childish nature of the political fight made it easy to satirize, as it was already so absurd that extreme exaggeration wasn't necessary. Anne Garefino, executive producer, noted that applying the election process to kindergarten made it "finally [make] sense," and Stone said the storyline "kind of wrote itself" when applied to children. The voices of the kindergarteners were provided by actual children, including the son of a show producer, and Parker and Stone enjoyed recording them because it was funny to hear real kids perform. The episode was produced with a team of 70 animators and computer engineers to meet the tight deadline. The episode was included in the UMD South Park: When Technology Attacks, released on October 11, 2005, alongside other episodes such as "Best Friends Forever," "Cancelled," "Simpsons Already Did It," and "Towelie." Critics praised the episode, with Alan Sepinwall and Matt Zoller Seitz calling it "terrific," especially the kindergarten election and recount scenes, and Bill Gibron calling it a "clever attack" on the Florida voting debacle, noting its sharp satire and fun Terminator-style elements. DVD Movie Guide's Colin Jacobson described it as a "clever riff" on Terminator and the 2000 election, calling both plots effective and the episode "funny and smart." IGN's David Galindo called it "great," and Lisa Davis of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram named Mr. Garrison's line "You're all acting like a bunch of kids!" the "best line of the week." The New York Post's Andrea Peyser noted that the class election ends in a deadlock, mirroring the deadlocked Florida vote, and that Rosie O'Donnell appears to gather lawyers, media, and friends to settle the race, paralleling her real-life petition to demand a revote in Palm Beach County. The episode's references to Florida and the state's undecided status are highlighted by the name Flora, one of the kindergarteners.
